name: Omar Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. We do not sell or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and still learning the invoice queue at a contact centre after secondary school. I answer morning calls, match invoice and delivery numbers, and sometimes ask a senior agent to check a credit; I use AI search once in a while after someone has tried it. I like getting a customer their correct bill, but a mismatched number can leave me staring at two screens while the queue grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to keep answering customers properly and let the new search box earn its place. A machine finding an old invoice is useful if an agent checks the number before speaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI search once in a while after another agent shows me where it helps, but I still stumble on the claims screen. We have about two months of bills saved and a mortgage, so a quiet year is welcome even if I cannot relax about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the morning call shifts and ask the senior agent to check my disputed invoices. In the first year of this plateau, I'd put a small part of each pay packet into the mortgage account before we spend on weekends out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the job, watchful about the bills. The school shoes still need replacing whether the search box works or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for another check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once mixed up an invoice number with the delivery number and promised a credit too early. The senior agent caught it, and now I read both numbers back before closing the call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner think about the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Amira likes having the mortgage money put aside first. We have two children at school. Two months of expenses saved could cover a short job gap, not a life without work.

S0.quote: Two months of expenses saved could cover a short job gap, not a life without work.
say: I would keep **answering customers** and let the search box prove useful.
I would have an agent check each **invoice number** before making a promise.
think: I use AI search sometimes but still need help with the **claims screen**.
I have about **two months** saved against a mortgage, so a quiet year still feels tight.
do: Keep the **morning shifts** and ask a senior agent to check disputed invoices.
Put a small part of each **pay packet** into the mortgage account.
feel: **Relieved** about work, still watchful about household bills.
fieldNote: Omar names a **mixed-up number** from his own calls, explaining his insistence on checking.
His **two-month reserve** is a pause for the family, not a reason to stop earning.

steps.text: Keep morning customer calls and check disputed invoices with a senior agent
Transfer part of each pay packet into a mortgage account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company can use a tool that works, but it must tell us what happens to the junior rota. I'd ask two other agents to bring our repeat-call counts to the supervisor together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine calls I am only just learning are the first ones a good reply system could take. If my hours drop, Amira's wage and two months saved will not carry the mortgage for long, even with some other centres nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down repeat calls for one week with two coworkers and bring the count to the supervisor. If the centre makes the new tool standard, I'd practise on ten closed cases with a senior agent; in the first year after rollout, if my shifts fall, I'd apply for a posted paid call job nearby only if its hours and wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn a tested call system, but I cannot promise my mortgage lender that I will learn fast enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the supervisor to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid practice time and a target that counts calls coming back, not just fast answers. A second call means the first number did not settle the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring coworkers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not want one junior agent called a complainer for showing the figures. If three of us sign the same note, the supervisor has to answer the shift rather than one person.

S1.quote: I can learn a tested call system, but I cannot promise my mortgage lender that I will learn fast enough.
say: I would accept a **tested tool** while asking what happens to junior shifts.
I would bring **repeat-call counts** with coworkers to the supervisor.
think: I see **routine calls** at risk before I have mastered them.
I know **two months saved** and one wage cannot carry our mortgage for long.
do: Count **repeat calls** with two coworkers and raise them together.
Practise ten **closed cases** with a senior agent on paid time if the AI tool becomes standard.
Apply for a **posted paid call job** if shifts fall and new hours and wages cover bills.
feel: **Anxious** about my learning pace and the mortgage.
fieldNote: Omar treats **shared figures** as a way to ask management about paid practice and targets.
He will learn AI only after **supervised old-case testing**, consistent with his measured approach.

steps.text: Count repeat calls with two coworkers and raise the figures together
Practise ten closed AI cases with senior agent on paid time if tool becomes standard
Apply for posted paid call work if shifts fall and wages and hours cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre to give us dates in writing and pay people for any training it asks us to take. I would not tell my children that a course link is a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 could answer even the awkward invoice calls better than I can. The robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031, but that delay does not save a headset shift. Two months saved will go quickly if both my wages and another centre's openings shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for written staffing dates now and cancel the family holiday. In the first year after AGI arrives, if my call role ends, I'd ask my cousin about a posted paid electrician apprentice place, but I would apply only if the wage covers our bills and the required classes are paid or affordable without using the mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. My cousin works for an electrical contractor, but I have no paid apprentice offer in my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your cousin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Tariq works with an electrical contractor and has told me what the first months are like. I would not ask for a family favour over another worker; I need a proper vacancy, safety training, and a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to a posted call role with enough hours as a bridge and ask Amira to sit with me over the budget. I would not pay for a certificate first and hope somebody might hire me later.

S2.quote: My cousin works for an electrical contractor, but I have no paid apprentice offer in my hand.
say: I would demand **written dates** and paid training before jobs change.
I would tell my family a **course link** is not a job.
think: I expect AGI could take **awkward invoice calls** by 2028.
I know **2031 robots** do not protect headset shifts, and two months saved could vanish fast.
do: Ask for **staffing dates** now and cancel the family holiday.
Apply for a **posted paid apprenticeship** after cuts only if wages cover bills and classes spare mortgage savings.
Apply for a posted **call role** as a bridge if no apprentice place exists and its hours cover bills.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a contact but no firm offer.
fieldNote: Omar treats his cousin as a **source of information**, not a guaranteed employer.
He requires **wages and affordable classes** before using an apprenticeship to support the mortgage.

steps.text: Cancel the family holiday to protect the mortgage account
Apply for posted paid apprenticeship after cuts if wages cover bills and classes avoid mortgage savings
Apply for a posted paid call role with bill-covering hours if no apprentice place exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to find out what paid apprenticeships exist, if we use the time. I'd also ask the centre to show the junior rota each year, not just talk about training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the harder invoice calls and save more before 2031. AGI would still do thinking work then; robots arrive around 2034, so even an electrical trade may change after I enter it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask Tariq to show me a full paid workday if his contractor allows it, and I'd keep my call shifts. If the contractor posts a paid apprentice place with wages and class fees that fit our mortgage budget, I'd apply and take the required classes; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd move only for a written offer with enough hours to cover bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not cornered. Five years lets me find out whether I can work on a building site all week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the workday tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see the early start, the ladder work, and what the apprentice is allowed to touch. A Saturday helping a relative is not the same as being paid to learn safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for classes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the contractor pays and whether the schedule fits our family. If it does not, I would keep the call wage and save rather than take money out of the mortgage account.

S3.quote: A Saturday helping a relative is not the same as being paid to learn safely.
say: I would check for **paid apprenticeships** while there is time.
I would ask for a **yearly junior rota** from the centre.
think: I could improve **invoice calls** and save more before AGI in 2031.
I see **2034 robots** as a reason to test an electrical trade carefully.
do: Ask for a **paid workday** with the electrical contractor if allowed.
Keep my **call shifts** while checking other work.
Apply for a **posted paid apprenticeship** and take classes only if wages and fees fit the mortgage budget.
feel: **Worried**, but able to inspect the trade before changing jobs.
fieldNote: Omar wants to see ladder work and **safety rules**, not rely on family stories.
He will keep a **call wage** if the apprentice package cannot cover bills and fees.

steps.text: Take a paid electrical trial day if the contractor permits it
Keep customer call shifts until a written paid offer arrives
Apply for posted paid apprenticeship if wages cover bills and class fees spare mortgage account
Take required classes only with written bill-covering offer, family-compatible hours and fees sparing mortgage savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to work and learn, but the centre still owes us honest rota numbers each year. My children cannot eat a promise about future jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 the mortgage might still be there, even if the children are grown. AGI in 2036 reaches our calls before hands-on robots around 2039; I should not wait until 2035 to find out what a trade pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my call shift and add a little to savings in months with full hours. Over the decade I'd ask Tariq once a year about posted paid apprentice places and try a paid day if one is offered; in the first year after 2036, I'd switch only for a written offer with hours and pay that cover our mortgage and school bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but able to make a slow plan. I can protect the job I have while looking at the work my cousin actually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow for a trade course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not without a paid place and a fee plan that leaves our mortgage account alone. I want the work first, then the class it requires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A signed offer with wages and hours that cover the household bills. I would not quit a real call shift for a promise from my cousin or my manager.

S4.quote: My children cannot eat a promise about future jobs.
say: I would ask for **honest yearly rota numbers** while keeping a wage.
I would remind colleagues that **future promises** do not pay school bills.
think: I may still have a **mortgage** at 53 in 2036.
I know **2039 robots** follow call-work AGI, so I need to check trade wages early.
do: Keep my **call shift** and save a little when hours are full.
Check for **posted paid apprenticeships** yearly and try a paid workday if offered.
Switch after 2036 only for a **written offer** with wages and hours covering bills.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to check a trade without losing current pay.
fieldNote: Omar would not borrow for a **trade course** without a paid place and fee plan.
He wants to judge **actual wages and hours**, not rely on a family promise.

steps.text: Keep customer call shifts while full hours remain
Add to savings in months with full call hours
Check posted paid apprenticeships yearly and try a paid day if offered
Switch after 2036 only for written wages and hours covering household bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I could lose call wages before finding a paid apprentice place, and our mortgage cannot wait through an unpaid course. Written staffing dates, a real posted opening, and training fees covered by the employer would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what an apprenticeship really pays in its first year. My cousin can open a conversation, but I still need wages and safe training on paper.

headlineQuote: My cousin can open a conversation, but I still need wages and safe training on paper.
portrait: Omar is a **43-year-old junior agent** learning invoice calls after secondary school, with a habit of checking numbers twice.
He has **typical pay**, about two months saved, a partner, two school-age children, a mortgage, and some nearby centres.
He uses AI **occasionally** once others prove it, and puts paid work and family bills ahead of a course title.
His cousin offers **electrical trade information**, but only a posted paid apprentice place could support a switch.
Fast **2028 AGI** alarms him; longer timelines let him test a workday and build savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove call wages before he finds a paid apprentice place that covers the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing dates**, a posted paid opening, and covered training fees would make a trade switch possible.
